lines: The observed variance structure is format-associated: MC benchmarks concentrate item-related variance at 68--72\%, while FF benchmarks disperse it to 31--41\%, with no overlap. Critically, even restricting to item difficulty alone (excluding model$\times$item DIF), MC benchmarks show 34--38\% versus FF 17--24\%, maintaining complete separation (unbundled benchmark-level $d = 4.84$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[2.32, 8.19]$), confirming that the format gap is not an artifact of DIF bundling. A permutation test on \texttt{item\_id} variance shares yields $p = 0.10$ ($n = 5$, $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ exhaustive permutations). The item-level effect size is tightly bounded (Cohen's $d = 1.73$; bootstrap 95\% CI $[1.72, 1.83]$), but the benchmark-level CI spans zero ($[-1.7, 5.1]$, noncentral $t$, $df = 3$), reflecting the inherent limitation of $n = 5$. With $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ possible MC/FF partitions under exhaustive permutation, $p = 0.10$ represents the resolution floor; rejecting at $\alpha = 0.05$ is mathematically impossible regardless of effect magnitude. We therefore present the format-associated pattern as a descriptive observation with strong item-level support ($d = 1.73$ [1.72, 1.83]) rather than a confirmatory finding. This structural difference does not extend to item budgets: GSM8K requires 128 items for $G \geq 0.80$---the highest of all benchmarks---while HellaSwag (MC, 118) exceeds both ARC (MC, 98) and MATH (FF, 101), demonstrating that format alone does not predict evaluation cost. Figure~\ref{fig:cross_benchmark} visualizes the contrast.

lines: The observed variance structure is format-associated: MC benchmarks concentrate item-related variance at 68--72\%, while FF benchmarks disperse it to 31--41\%, with no overlap. Critically, even restricting to item difficulty alone (excluding model$\times$item DIF), MC benchmarks show 34--38\% versus FF 17--24\%, maintaining complete separation (unbundled benchmark-level $d = 4.84$, bootstrap 95\% CI $[2.32, 8.19]$), confirming that the format gap is not an artifact of DIF bundling. A permutation test yields $p = 0.10$ ($\binom{5}{3} = 10$ exhaustive partitions), the resolution floor---rejecting at $\alpha = 0.05$ is impossible regardless of effect magnitude. The item-level effect size is tightly bounded ($d = 1.73$; 95\% CI $[1.72, 1.83]$), but the benchmark-level CI spans zero ($[-1.7, 5.1]$, $df = 3$). We therefore present the format-associated pattern as a descriptive observation with strong item-level support rather than a confirmatory finding. This does not extend to item budgets: GSM8K requires 128 items for $G \geq 0.80$ while HellaSwag (MC, 118) exceeds both ARC (98) and MATH (101), showing that format alone does not predict evaluation cost. Figure~\ref{fig:cross_benchmark} visualizes the contrast.

-One might argue the format gap is tautological: MC constrains generation noise, mechanically inflating item-related shares. Two observations argue against this. First, HellaSwag is MC yet model$\times$item (36.0\%) exceeds item (34.3\%)---pure format effects would produce uniform item dominance. Second, within MMLU's 57 subjects, difficulty dispersion correlates with item variance ($\rho = 0.806$, $p = 0.005$, $n = 10$), and \texttt{high\_school\_mathematics} (open-ended numerical items) shows item variance of just 10.4\%, below GSM8K (16.9\%). This extends across benchmarks: cross-benchmark $\text{std}(p_i)$ correlates with \texttt{item\_id} share ($\rho = 0.82$, $p = 0.089$, $n = 5$; Appendix~\ref{app:difficulty_scatter}), with MC benchmarks showing higher dispersion ($0.27$--$0.31$) than FF ($0.22$--$0.23$). Format constrains the noise floor, but item difficulty heterogeneity determines the magnitude of item-related variance within that floor.
